content.thinking:
Now that I've reviewed the docs, I need to design the red panda component and write it to samples/redPanda.ts, making sure to check relative import paths for the builder and kits. I'll iteratively verify with typecheck and preview tools as I build it out.

For the pose, I'm planning a red panda standing on all fours atop a mossy boulder, with its tail arched in an S-curve for balance and legs slightly splayed—a neutral, riggable stance. I need to work out the skeleton hierarchy, deciding whether the stone is a separate prop bound to a root joint, with the panda's hips as a child joint beneath it.

Now I'm calculating actual coordinates: stone top surface at roughly y=0.30, panda feet resting there, leg length around 0.17m, putting the body center near y=0.52.

I'm placing the hips further back and the shoulders forward, with the head large and forward-positioned for cuteness, and the tail curving up and back from the hips with bushy proportions and ring stripes. For the pose, I'm widening the stance and spreading the forelegs slightly for balance, with the tail arcing upward in an S-curve, and starting to lay out the spine chain from the hips.

Mapping spine curve points...

I'm reconsidering the hierarchy: rather than making "hips" the root joint (which would move the stone when hips posed), I'll separate a neutral "root" joint at the origin for the stone, with "hips" as a child joint at P0 carrying the spine role.

For the body sweep, I'm figuring out how to chain bones through the loft—thinking of using a bone list like [tail, hips, spine, head] so the sweep follows joints and chains together. I'll build a single "spine" chain parented to hips, starting just past P0 to avoid redundant overlap with the hips joint itself.

Simplifying further: hips sits at P0, spine chain grows from there with three joints parented to hips, and a separate neck chain runs from chest to head. Since chain joint names can be arbitrary, I realize I can just name the first spine joint "hips" directly and skip the separate root joint complication.

For the neck, I'll use a 3-point path giving two spans with names ending in "head" as the tip joint, parented to the spine's tip. The head joint then becomes the parent for the jaw and other head features like ears, with orientation aimed along the neck's tangent so it faces forward.

I'm shaping the neck path so the final tangent points mostly forward with a slight upward tilt, placing the head joint at the path's end and using local direction words like forward/up/left for the head's orientation rather than raw axes, since the tilt is minor. Now I'm planning the red panda's head shape itself—broad and round with a short muzzle.

For the face details, I'm settling on a black nose, white muzzle and cheek patches, large triangular ears with fluffy white rims, reddish-brown fur, white eyebrow marks, and dark tear-track lines. I'm also deciding on Genshin-style big anime eyes using decals, debating iris color—leaning toward an amber-gold or teal tone that contrasts nicely against the red-orange coat.

Now I'm positioning the eye decal onto the skull sphere, sizing it relative to the head radius, and deciding whether to keep a faint blush accent since it might still suit the red panda's coloring.

I'll settle on "#ff9a8a" for the blush tone, and disable the drawn eyebrow stroke in favor of white eyebrow patches instead, while keeping the lash flicks. For the skull shape, I'm scaling a sphere to form a wide head, then building fluffy cream-colored cheek tufts using extruded zig-zag shapes placed on either side to mimic the red panda's characteristic cheek fluff.

Mirroring the outline across the x-axis so each side faces outward with a slight downward point, I'm giving the tufts some thickness along the z-axis to keep them flat but stylized, like layered plates rather than fully rounded fur.

Now I'm planning the texture set, aiming for roughly 5-12: an anime-style eye for the kit, moss tuft cards clustered like leaf blades on the stone, cream/orange fur tuft cards for cheeks and tail edges, and maybe a small glowing glyph decal on the stone for a Genshin-like touch. I'm also considering adding a few tiny glowing Dendro-style mushrooms near the stone base for extra atmosphere.

For the glowing rune, I realize decals only attach to meshes, not planes, so I'll place it as a separate glowing plane positioned just above the stone surface instead. I'm also thinking through face details—nose, mouth line, and tear-track markings—deciding whether to handle these as position-based paints on the skull mesh using a closure that takes the head center as a parameter, or as simpler decal textures.

Now I'm weighing a face-mask SVG decal approach versus painting the face directly with a paint function: the decal would cover white eyebrow spots, white muzzle, dark tear lines, and the nose all at once, but I need two decal layers (face mask and eyes) at slightly different lift depths to avoid z-fighting, settling on roughly 1.5mm separation. As an alternative I'm considering painting the skull with a coat function for the base rust-orange and layering white on the lower face via some kind of fur-edge paint technique instead.

zle needs a separate cream-white snout piece protruding forward from the head, scaled small with a black nose sphere at its tip, plus a lower jaw wedge on the jaw joint for the mouth. For ears, I'm planning large rounded triangular shapes, rust-colored outside with white fur inside edges, placed at the top sides of the head tilting outward.

Computing ear orientation vectors...

Actually I'm reconsidering the approach entirely—rather than fiddling with extrude outline normals, I'll model ears as squashed, tilted spheres (hemispheric puppet-style) with a smaller inner white sphere offset forward for the inner ear detail.

I'm adding a cream-colored inner ear sphere positioned slightly forward, and considering simple tuft details along the rim before deciding to keep it minimal. For the body, I'm aiming for a toon-shaded, cel-style fur coat finish typical of stylized character models.

For coloring I'm planning the red panda's natural palette: rust-red back, dark chestnut belly and chest, black-brown stocking legs fading in from a set height, cream-white face patches, and a ringed tail alternating rust and dark stripes, using the vertical position to drive the gradient transitions between zones.

Adding mottled fur texture and tail stripe banding...

Working out the tail's path from hips curling upward in an S-arch, sizing it stylized and fluffy at roughly 0.65 length, with a tapered radius function that bulges in the middle and thins toward the tip.

Now I'm sizing up the stone pedestal beneath the panda's feet, making it an elongated boulder roughly 0.75 long by 0.6 wide with a flat-ish top to support the footprint spread, built from clustered scaled spheres with a mossy paint finish.

Instead I'll build the boulder from a rotated LatheGeometry profile scaled non-uniformly for elongation, with flat shading for a faceted look. For the paint function I'll blend moss green on upward-facing normals with added noise against a cool grey-blue stone base elsewhere, aiming for that stylized cel-shaded Genshin rock look.

Then I'll add small accent details on top: tiny moss blade cards sticking up, a handful of cute little flowers (simple cone-petal shapes in pink/white), and maybe small glowing mushrooms for extra charm.

For accessories I'll add a teal-and-gold ribbon collar with a small gold charm medallion and glowing gem, plus flowing tassel tails that sweep behind as the panda moves on all fours, keeping it Genshin-cute but subtle so the panda stays the focus. I'm also considering a single leaf accent on the head for a touch of whimsy.

Now shifting to leg rigging: placing front shoulder and hip joints with IK, working out foot positions and leg segment lengths so the limbs bend naturally. Since red pandas are plantigrade rather than digitigrade, I'm deciding whether to use two or three segments per hind leg to get believable proportions.

Each leg becomes a tapered tube swept along its joint chain, with paws built as flattened dark spheres plus four small toe bumps and tiny cream-colored claw cones at the tips.

I'm coloring the legs with a gradient from rust at the upper thigh into dark chestnut toward the paw, running along the y-axis for symmetry. For foot placement, I need the paw ball resting right at the stone's top surface with a slight sink-in for contact realism, and I have to keep the moss card decorations away from the foot zones so they don't clip through the paws.

Overall the model stands around 1.05 tall at the tail and 0.75 at the head, with the stone base resting flush at y=0. For the body, I'm planning to use a sweep along a combined spine-and-neck path with varying elliptical radii to get a chunky hip-to-shoulder taper, using a catmull-rom curve for the path.

Rather than fusing spine and neck into one continuous sweep, I'm opting for two separate sweeps that match radii at the junction (around 0.095) so the seam blends naturally, with the neck narrowing further toward the head.

The head and ruff will cover most of the neck anyway, so the seam is largely hidden. I'm varying the spine radius along its length—wider at hips and chest, tapering toward the ends—and adding a dark brown chest bib with proper fur edges, plus separate haunch spheres at the hip joints to bulk up the thighs.

Now working through the head details: cream cheek tufts, rust forehead with lighter mottling, a protruding cream muzzle with a nose, and setting up the skull sphere proportions and local head offsets for precise face geometry placement.

Adjusting head sizing to be a bit bigger and chibi-like relative to the body, then computing eye decal placement using azimuth and elevation angles against the skull ellipsoid surface to position them symmetrically.

For the mask decal, I'm figuring out the hit point, normal direction, and size so it faces correctly given the head's slight upward tilt from neck to crown — tweaking the neck endpoint coordinates to reduce that tilt angle.

Now I'm checking body proportions: with the body center and radius set, the belly and feet positions leave short, chunky legs with just enough length to bend naturally. I'm setting up the leg limb chains with root and target positions, lengths, and bend direction to compute reach distances for the IK.

I'm positioning the paw as a small sphere offset forward from the IK target, placing four tiny toe spheres with small cream cone claws along the front, and solving for the target height so the paw bottom sits flush with the ground.

Now I'm naming the joint chains: front legs use shoulder-elbow-paw names per side (FL/FR), tail attaches to the hips joint with 5-6 segments for a smooth catmull curve, and ears get their own small hinge joints under the head with parts attached.

For the jaw, I'm adding a joint under the head angled slightly forward and down, with a small cream sphere for the lower jaw and a thin dark interior piece to suggest a closed mouth gap beneath the snout.

Now I'm planning whiskers as thin cream sticks extending from the muzzle with a few per side, plus a cute forehead tuft made from curved tapered sweeps in rust with cream tips, like a small ahoge, along with some leaf-shaped tufts pointing up and back.

For the cheek ruffs I'm sketching spiky cream outlines extruded with a bit of thickness on both sides of the head, positioning them near the cheek area and tilting them outward and back so they flare naturally from the face.

I'm keeping the fur color mostly cream, maybe with a subtle gradient toward orange at the outer tips. Now I'm scattering moss tuft cards across the top and rim regions, filtering out spots too close to the paws and using two moss texture variants for visual variety, before moving on to shaping the stone boulder form underneath.

For the boulder itself, I'm adding a few smaller fused rocks and pebbles using faceted icosahedron shapes at the base for a natural clustered look, then placing a glowing cyan rune glyph (circle with leaf symbols) as a decal on the boulder's front face, using an emissive texture material so it glows against the stone surface.

I'm also adding a second rune on the left side, plus a small gold medallion charm with a glowing gem hanging from a collar loop around the panda's neck, working out where the neck chain joints sit relative to the head and ruff.

Rethinking the placement — maybe the collar should wrap the chest/shoulders instead of the neck, since it would hide under the chin and ruff anyway. I'm considering looping a cutting plane across the spine sweep near its end, using a chain point as an oriented frame to slice through for the collar.

Let me budget out part counts per section: body sweeps and haunches around 8, legs at roughly 11 parts each for paws/toes/claws/fur totaling ~44, tail with fluff tufts and dark tip around a dozen, head details like skull, snout, ears, whiskers and decals near 40, scarf about 12, and the stone plus moss and flowers adding another dozen or more.

I'm thinking total part count lands near 160+, and I want to add fur tuft cards at the chest edge, elbows, and haunches for a fluffy look while keeping it restrained in Genshin style — one textured card per fur spot rather than a full coat. I also need to settle on which textures get colored directly versus tinted grey drawings, since colored drawings carry their own colors and can't be tinted like plain grey ones.

So I'll make the tuft texture a grey gradient so it can be tinted by the card's paint, and I'm adding a simple flower texture (white petals, yellow center) rendered as a small cross of cards for tiny 3D flowers. That brings my texture set to eye, mask, moss A, moss B, rune, tuft, and flower, plus whatever else comes next.

For glowing mushrooms, I'll use a lathe-dome cap with a flat glow color and cream stems, clustering three small ones near the stone base. Since there's no real outline shader available, I'll skip the bold ink-outline look except maybe using inkLines as a rim accent around the snout, and I'll keep painted parts sharing one paint sheet while flat-color parts like the claws stay within the 64-colour limit.

Now I'm setting up the imports for the build script, pulling in geometry, math, paint, and toon-shading helpers, and defining the rust color palette for the creature's material.

I'm defining STONE and MOSS cel palettes with mottled texture, then building a combined stone-with-moss paint that blends moss coverage based on surface normal and vertical position so moss appears on upward-facing areas.

Now I'm setting up body geometry constants and spine points for the creature's skeleton.

I could instead apply a small forward-tilt rotation to the head joint after building, around 15-20°, so it levels out relative to the neck sweep's natural upward tangent -- posing it after the neck chain is built so the sweep geometry still follows the unposed chain. Alternatively, I could just add a fourth point to the neck path to directly control the end tangent rather than relying on a post-build rotation.

Let me work out where the head sits: with the neck spanning into neck1/neck2/neck3 and a flat tip, the head joint lands around z=0.34, making the head center roughly z=0.40, y=0.61ish, with the skull extending from about 0.295 to 0.505 -- stretching well forward of the front paws at z=0.21. That's a fairly exaggerated forward reach for the head, though it reads as appealingly oversized. I'm weighing whether to just shift the whole body forward to balance the proportions instead.

Checking the stone's footprint so the panda's paws land within its radius, and working out limb root positions for shoulders and hips to match the pose.

Still placing leg sweeps and radius tapers, tracing the hind leg knee bend from hip down to the foot position.

Simpler complex limb returns will work fine. For front legs I'll use 2 segments bending backward at the elbow, then build a paw function that places a flattened sphere body at the target with small toe bumps offset toward the front, keeping toes dark and compact.

For claws I'll add tiny cream spikes angled forward-down, skipping any fur tufts or lighter sock fur on the legs to keep things simple. For body paint I'm setting up a fur edge transition between rust and dark tones with a toothed, zigzagging boundary running along the z-axis to mimic a jagged belly line.

Writing paint function logic...

Now I'm figuring out the head coat colors, keeping the skull rust-toned with cream cheeks and placing the dark tear lines, then mapping the mask decal's SVG coordinates to world-space eye positions.

I'll give the eye decals a slightly outward-tilted direction vector using the ray hit point as the anchor, accepting the mild foreshortening. For the mask, I'm planning the white muzzle puffs as ellipses near the cheeks, then extending white patches down toward the muzzle protrusion with a zigzag-edged polygon plus eyebrow highlights.

I'm adding small rotated ellipse spots above the eyes and considering a darker forehead "M" marking like real red pandas have, along with curved dark brown tear lines running from under the eyes down toward the muzzle, mirrored on both sides. Since the decal uses standard lighting while the skull is cel-shaded, I'm weighing whether to instead paint these markings directly onto the skull's surface based on position so the shading style matches, using local coordinate regions to place the white patches and tear-line curves.

Writing paint function code...

I'm marking a dark tear-line path running from the inner eye down toward the muzzle, then keeping the forehead a paler rust tone above the cream lower face. I'm computing face paint in model space with the head fixed in build pose, using forward-facing normals and position checks so the cream extends onto the snout protrusion, and aligning the eye decals symmetrically around the center line.

Checking the eye placement against the skull's curved width at that height, the decals fit comfortably within the visible front surface without wrapping past the edges. For the decal raycasting, I need to make sure it only hits the skull surface itself and not the cheek ruff or other parts layered in front.

For the eye direction, I'll set an explicit normal tilt outward matching the eye's horizontal position, and use mirror to flip the kit's default right-eye asset onto the left side. Now I'm moving on to shaping the nose as a scaled sphere.

Working out snout geometry...

Still positioning the ears...

Now I'm adding the forehead ahoge tuft as curved rust-colored blade sweeps from the skull top, plus whiskers as thin tapered cream rods from the snout, and starting on the brow details.

For the scarf, I'm defining a loop around the torso's spine sweep surface, positioning it near the chest where the legs sprout, so I need to be careful the band placement doesn't collide awkwardly with the leg geometry.

This placement works well as a collar-scarf sitting at the neck/chest junction, covering that transition point. I'm planning the scarf as a teal cloth band (around #1fa3a8) with thin gold trim lines along both edges for a stripe-like cel-shaded look.

For the geometry, I'm thinking of making it a puffy fat-tube loop swept around the neck at two different points for thickness, then adding a knot at the front-left with two ribbon tails hanging down and curving outward using a membrane between bezier edges for a flat ribbon effect, colored to match the teal and gold scheme.

Rather than having the ribbons dangle flatly down the chest, which wouldn't suit a four-legged pose, I'm reconsidering a streamer design flowing back from the nape over the back like a cape tail, curving with implied wind movement.

For the medallion, I'm figuring out placement — a small gold disc near the front chest below the collar, trying to position it low enough that it doesn't collide with the chin or head geometry.

I'm planning it as gold cylinder disc with a glowing teal gem center and two small connecting loops to the collar, then moving on to tail detailing: ring paint along the sweep, tufts as cards near the edges, and a darker tip blended in with banding.

For fur I'm adding sparse leaf-shaped tuft cards tinted by the tail's paint color, plus a few extra fluff cards at the chest, haunch, and elbow. For the ground stone I'm scattering mossy grass tufts, tiny white-pink flower cards, a few glowing mushrooms, and hanging moss vine cards along the front.

Now I'm placing hanging moss tassels along the boulder's top rim, sampling points along a loop at the upper edge and orienting each card facing upward with a 180 lean so they drape downward, checking how they intersect the sloped wall near the shoulder.

Since the wall bulges outward below the rim, straight-down cards would get buried, so I'm offsetting the loop outward by a small lift along the surface normal to keep them clear before adding a few more. For the overall stone, I'm building it from a main boulder lathe shape plus a front-left bump, a back-right bump, and scattered base pebbles.

I'm defining the lathe profile points from bottom center up to the top, checking that the winding order produces outward-facing normals as in typical Three.js examples, and scaling the stone part slightly deeper in z to give it more volume.

The plateau radius at the top is too small to fit paws without clipping into the sloped shoulder, so I'm widening the profile's upper points and increasing the z-scale to give the flat top enough room for the paws to sit properly.

Checking the proportions, the boulder was coming out too large relative to the panda's body, so I'm scaling down the stone's radii by 0.8 and adjusting the z-depth to keep paw placement within the tapered plateau — this brings the stone to a more believable "balancing" size relative to the panda.

Now I'm adjusting the leg stance to sell the balancing pose better, splaying the front paws outward like arms while confirming they still fall within the elliptical plateau boundary of the stone's top surface.

Before writing the actual file, I want to double-check the SDK's API shapes — the chain function's parent/role options, skeleton part options, and how cards, membrane, and decal are configured — so I'll quickly grep the source and peek at a sample file for correct imports and structure.

input.command: ls samples | head -30; ls scratch 2>/dev/null | head; cat package.json | head -30
